clue.text: It may feature repeating arguments once or twice -or thrice, perhaps

definitions.text: It may feature repeating arguments once or twice

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of the following words might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A note on how often a debater restates a point: once, twice or maybe three times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals that the letters of OR THRICE are rearranged; the definition describes the art of persuasive speech, which favours repetition.
explanation.definitionFit: The art of persuasive oratory often uses deliberate repetition of points for effect.

clue.text: Higgins is one, Chesterton said

parts.note: quotes G K Chesterton's poem The Song of the Strange Ascetic, whose refrain says Higgins is an unbeliever, a pagan

explanation.surface: A reported remark by Chesterton about a man called Higgins.
explanation.walkthrough: The line comes from Chesterton's poem The Song of the Strange Ascetic, which contrasts a pagan's pleasures with the joyless habits of the godless Higgins.
explanation.definitionFit: Chesterton's poem labels Higgins a pagan, someone outside the Christian faith.

clue.text: Terrible tosh clued as "old satire"

indicators.note: something terrible is a mess, so the letters of these words are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A reviewer dismissing a crossword clue that calls something an old satire as awful rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' signals the anagram of TOSH CLUED; the answer is Aristophanes's comedy mocking Socrates.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristophanes's comedy of 423 BC is an ancient Greek satire lampooning Socrates.

clue.text: Concerning characters, process words again

parts.note: re is a short word meaning about or concerning
type means printed characters or letters

explanation.surface: Advice about reworking a document's letters on a word processor.
explanation.definitionFit: Keying a text in a second time on a typewriter or computer.

clue.text: Rascal is confounded by strange earl who introduces Richardson heroine

indicators.note: confounded means thrown into confusion, so the letters of rascal is are muddled
strange signals the letters of earl who are made odd by rearrangement

explanation.surface: A villain is baffled by an odd nobleman who brings in a character from Samuel Richardson.
explanation.walkthrough: Two separate anagrams: 'confounded' acts on RASCAL IS and 'strange' on EARL WHO, giving the first name and surname in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Samuel Richardson's epistolary novel of 1748 is its tragic heroine.

clue.text: Like the speech of Archibald MacLeish

definitions.text: Like the speech of Archibald MacLeish

parts.words: Like the speech of Archibald MacLeish
parts.note: alludes to the title of MacLeish's 1936 verse collection, describing its speech as open and addressed to everyone

explanation.surface: A comparison with the way the American poet Archibald MacLeish talked.
explanation.walkthrough: MacLeish published a book of poems called Public Speech in 1936, so the speech in the clue is the open, communal kind.
explanation.definitionFit: MacLeish's 1936 collection title pairs speech with the adjective meaning open to all people.

clue.text: John Collier's were in the fire

definitions.text: John Collier's were in the fire

parts.words: John Collier's were in the fire
parts.note: refers to John Collier's 1958 story collection whose title speaks of images seen in the flames

explanation.surface: Something belonging to John Collier ended up burned in a fire.
explanation.walkthrough: John Collier's short-story collection is titled Pictures in the Fire; the surface suggests his property was burned.
explanation.definitionFit: Collier's book title names the images people imagine seeing in glowing flames.

clue.text: Governor of Messina puts sign on collective security group

indicators.note: in a down answer, one piece put on another sits above it

parts.note: Leo is a sign of the zodiac
NATO is the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a collective defence alliance

explanation.surface: An official in Sicily adds a symbol to a military alliance.
explanation.walkthrough: Leonato is the governor of Messina and Hero's father in Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: In Much Ado About Nothing this character rules the Sicilian city where the play is set.

clue.text: Poet portrays old king with high pressure

parts.note: Old King Cole is the merry monarch of the nursery rhyme
a ridge is a narrow area of high atmospheric pressure in weather forecasting

explanation.surface: A poet's work depicts an aged monarch under great strain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high pressure' looks like stress but is a meteorological term; Old King Cole is from the nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Taylor Coleridge wrote The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, a Romantic poem.

clue.text: Halt book for sad poem

parts.note: halt is an old word for lame or limping
NT, the New Testament, is a book of the Bible

explanation.surface: An instruction to stop reading and turn to a melancholy poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Halt' looks like an order to stop but is the old adjective for limping.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy or dirge expresses grief and mourning in verse.

clue.text: Differences between me and Wordsworth… occasioned in great part by the wicked folly of the—-—Montagu " (Coleridge, Letters)

definitions.text: Differences between me and Wordsworth… occasioned in great part by the wicked folly of the—-—Montagu " (Coleridge, Letters)

parts.words: Differences between me and Wordsworth… occasioned in great part by the wicked folly of the—-—Montagu " (Coleridge, Letters)
parts.note: a quotation from Coleridge's letters with a gap for the hyphenated insult he applied to Basil Montagu, meaning a supreme idiot

explanation.surface: Coleridge blames his quarrel with Wordsworth on Basil Montagu's meddling.
explanation.walkthrough: Basil Montagu repeated Wordsworth's private criticisms to Coleridge in 1810, causing their rift; the missing word fills the gap in Coleridge's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The hyphenated insult means a chief idiot, the greatest of all fools.

clue.text: A letter from Athens reaches Macedonian king in Antony's victory

indicators.note: one piece reaches another by arriving after it, so the Greek letter follows the king

parts.note: Philip II was king of Macedon and father of Alexander the Great
pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A message from Athens gets to the Macedonian ruler during Mark Antony's triumph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A letter' suggests a piece of correspondence but is a Greek alphabet letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius at this Macedonian battle in 42 BC.

clue.text: "Those hours …/ Will play the tyrants to the very same, / And that — which fairly doth excel" (Shakespeare, Sonnets)

definitions.text: "Those hours …/ Will play the tyrants to the very same, / And that — which fairly doth excel" (Shakespeare, Sonnets)

parts.words: "Those hours …/ Will play the tyrants to the very same, / And that — which fairly doth excel" (Shakespeare, Sonnets)
parts.note: a passage from Shakespeare's Sonnet 5 with a gap for the word meaning made ugly, played against fairly

explanation.surface: Lines from Shakespeare's fifth sonnet about time spoiling beauty.
explanation.walkthrough: In Sonnet 5 time will make ugly ('un-fair', a verb here) the beauty which now excels in fairness.
explanation.definitionFit: In the sonnet the word is a verb meaning to strip of beauty, the opposite of making lovely.

clue.text: Extremes not in Shakespearean actor

parts.note: the extremes of the globe are its poles, south and north, S and N
out means not at home, not in

explanation.surface: The far ends of something are missing from a performer of Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Snout the tinker is one of the amateur actors who play Pyramus and Thisbe in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: The tinker in A Midsummer Night's Dream performs the part of Wall in the mechanicals' play.

clue.text: Somerset Maugham's conclusion

explanation.surface: A description of how the novelist Somerset Maugham ended things.
explanation.definitionFit: Maugham's 1938 memoir has this title, and a final review of points closes a speech or trial.

clue.text: Was he a camera?

parts.note: plays on the opening of Goodbye to Berlin, 'I am a camera', later the title of a play from the book

explanation.surface: A puzzled question whether some man was a photographic device.
explanation.walkthrough: The Berlin narrator of Goodbye to Berlin says 'I am a camera'; John Van Druten's play from it was titled I Am a Camera.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist wrote Goodbye to Berlin, whose narrator describes himself as a recording camera.

clue.text: Log cabin for Emma?

parts.note: a log is a piece of timber, wood
a cabin is a small house

explanation.surface: A rustic hut built for a woman named Emma.
explanation.walkthrough: Emma is Jane Austen's heroine, whose surname is the answer; the question mark marks the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's heroine is called by this family name in Emma.

clue.text: French writer -down to earth — is arable in a way

indicators.note: in a way suggests the letters are taken in a different manner, rearranged

explanation.surface: A French author with earthy tastes is described as being fit for ploughing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' signals the anagram of IS ARABLE; the earthy Gargantua author fits the joke about farmland.
explanation.definitionFit: François Rabelais, Renaissance author of Gargantua and Pantagruel, is famed for coarse earthy humour.

clue.text: Feature of Amis's biographer

parts.note: refers to Kingsley Amis's 1995 novel about a biographer, titled after the facial hair he wears

explanation.surface: A characteristic of the man who wrote the life of Amis.
explanation.walkthrough: Kingsley Amis's last-but-one novel is The Biographer's Moustache; 'feature' is a facial one.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley Amis's novel names its biographer's upper-lip whiskers in its title.

clue.text: Steal scene in a coach to London?

explanation.surface: Someone stealing attention while travelling by coach towards the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Travel towards London is traditionally 'up', so a stagecoach heading there is going up by stage.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw attention from fellow performers; also travelling up to the capital by stagecoach.

clue.text: Code for a policeman

explanation.surface: A secret cipher meant for a constable.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Morse's dot-and-dash signalling code; also Colin Dexter's Oxford detective inspector.

clue.text: Somehow arm US's first-class warriors

indicators.note: somehow suggests these letters are put together in some other order

parts.note: taken as written
the United States, taken as written
A1 means first-class, with the 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: Somehow equip America's top-rank fighters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' signals the anagram of ARM, US and AI (A1, first-class, with the figure 1 read as I).
explanation.definitionFit: The hereditary military caste of feudal Japan were sword-bearing fighting men.

clue.text: Reception of a large volume, with hot content by Vidal

indicators.note: content means contained, so the abbreviation for hot sits within the book

parts.note: a tome is a large heavy book
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A party celebrating a big new book of passionate material by Gore Vidal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' is read as contained, not pleased. 'by Vidal' points to Gore Vidal's essay collection of the same title (1988).
explanation.definitionFit: A formal party held in one's own house for invited guests.

clue.text: Intimate view of Burgess's poet

parts.note: alludes to Anthony Burgess's 1963 novel about the poet Enderby, whose title promises a look within him

explanation.surface: A close-up portrait of the poet Anthony Burgess created.
explanation.walkthrough: Burgess's novel Inside Mr Enderby is about the poet F X Enderby.
explanation.definitionFit: Burgess's title puts the word meaning within before the poet's name, offering a view of his inner life.

clue.text: Aristocrat may offer one like that, in doggerel

definitions.text: Aristocrat may offer one like that, in doggerel

parts.words: Aristocrat may offer one like that, in doggerel
parts.note: the end of the word aristocrat chimes with the name of a rodent, a cheap pairing fit for doggerel

explanation.surface: A nobleman might produce such a thing in bad verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Aristo-CRAT ends with the sound of a rodent's name, the kind of easy rhyme found in doggerel.
explanation.definitionFit: A crude pairing of a rodent's name with a word that ends the same way, typical of bad verse.

clue.text: Tango air composed for merchant's friend

indicators.note: composed means put together, so the letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: A dance tune written for a trader's companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' suggests music for the tango but signals the anagram; the friend is Antonio's in The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Merchant of Venice this talkative character is a companion of Antonio and Bassanio.

clue.text: Old, disorganized revue seen as work of art

indicators.note: disorganized means out of order, so the letters of revue are scrambled

explanation.surface: An old, badly staged theatrical show is regarded as an artistic achievement.
explanation.definitionFit: A French borrowing for an artist's body of work or a single creative piece.

clue.text: The Miller's Tale (1953)

parts.note: points to a 1953 novel by Henry Miller, the middle book of his Rosy Crucifixion trilogy, not Chaucer

explanation.surface: Looks like Chaucer's Canterbury story, oddly dated to 1953.
explanation.walkthrough: Chaucer's Miller's Tale is the false path; the date shows the miller is Henry Miller, whose 1953 novel completes Sexus and Nexus.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Miller's 1953 novel is the second part of The Rosy Crucifixion trilogy.

clue.text: Former example with points is explanation

parts.note: ex means former, as in an ex-wife
e.g. is the abbreviation for for example
E and S are compass points, east and south

explanation.surface: A one-time instance with several argument points serves as clarification.
explanation.definitionFit: Critical interpretation of a text, especially of scripture.
